scenes.title: Three Patterns to Avoid
scenes.summary: Neither decent men falling into misfortune, nor the wicked rising, nor the villain falling: none arouses both pity, felt for the undeserving, and fear, felt for one like us.

scenes.title: The Man Between
scenes.summary: The tragic hero is neither outstanding in virtue nor brought down by vice, but falls through some error, a man of great fortune like Oedipus and Thyestes.

scenes.title: The Few Houses
scenes.summary: The fine plot is single and moves from good fortune to bad through great error; the finest tragedies concern a few houses: Alcmaeon, Oedipus, Orestes, Meleager, Thyestes, Telephus.

scenes.title: Euripides, Most Tragic
scenes.summary: Those who blame Euripides for his unhappy endings are wrong: such plays seem most tragic on the stage, and Euripides, whatever his faults, the most tragic of the poets.

scenes.title: The Double Plot
scenes.summary: The double structure of the Odyssey, good ends for the good and bad for the bad, pleases weak audiences; it belongs to comedy, where even Orestes and Aegisthus leave as friends.
